main_message: America stopped building small 2-4 unit corner buildings because three overlapping rule sets (zoning maps, single-stair fire codes, and mortgage lending categories) each block them, so fixing one isn't enough. The video leans toward 'the buildings are fine, the rules are the problem', but hedges a lot.
why_hook: The 1-in-13 versus 1-in-100 contrast is a concrete, surprising gap and the question 'why did we stop' is clear. It's a bit stat-heavy and flat, with no human or visual image yet.
mechanisms_in_your_words: Three 'locks': (1) zoning maps from Euclid/Hoover-era model law that bar small multifamily and mixed-use and add parking mandates; (2) building code that caps single-stair buildings at 3 stories, so a second stair eats small lots; (3) lending rules that split at 4 units, with mixed-use and 5-49 unit buildings falling into a financing gap. Together they squeeze the middle, so only big buildings and single-family houses get built.
ending_comment: Yes, it circles back to the corner building and the three rules, though it says 'in a growing number of places the first two are starting to' without showing results, so the payoff is thin.

boring_or_slow.why: Heavy on dates, committees and court history, like a lecture
Statistics for Colorado and Connecticut stacked one after another
Alphabet soup of Fannie, FHA, Freddie, Millennial Housing Commission, and fine-print rules
A list of states and dates that reads like a legal roundup

confusing.quote: Five homes or more, and a project moves into multifamily
confusing.why: Never says clearly how the 2-4 unit building gets financed today, or why 5-49 is a gap if it's 'multifamily'
Unclear how the three locks produce the squeeze versus other factors like costs and land prices
Logic is asserted, not shown. The evidence is on zoning only, so it doesn't actually test the stair or bank locks

confusing.quote: A fourth story? Not permitted with one stair
confusing.why: Doesn't say how this matters for a 2-4 unit building, which is usually 2-3 stories and already allowed one stair

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: on a small corner lot, it's a slice of every floor
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: Cost framing relies on Pew and a pro-reform nonprofit, with fire-service pushback only in the next segment
The quote makes the 1926 zoning logic look snobbish and sets the tone for the whole 'locks' framing

felt_biased_or_one_sided.quote: the first two are starting to
felt_biased_or_one_sided.why: Ends on reform momentum, even though the evidence in 08 says reform has produced very little

lean_detail: It tries to be balanced (Minneapolis results, fire chiefs, Sterling Heights opposition), but the 'locks' metaphor assumes the rules are obstacles to be opened. The 'each rule has its defenders' line feels like a perfunctory nod.
blame_detail: Blame goes to rules and institutions. Hoover and the Euclid decision are named but not villainized, and fire chiefs are presented as having a legitimate view.

claims_you_doubt.quote: Not because the building stopped working
claims_you_doubt.why: Asserted with no evidence on costs, land prices, labor or why developers prefer big buildings. The video itself shows zoning reform barely moved production

claims_you_doubt.quote: That's our calculation from Census completions
claims_you_doubt.why: The 1973 versus 2025 comparison ignores overall volume changes and other drivers like rising costs, so the causal link to the 'locks' is an inference

claims_you_doubt.quote: Each one, on its own, has a reason
claims_you_doubt.why: Called balanced, but the video then treats the three rules as the explanation of the decline

claims_you_doubt.quote: the missing second stair played no role in any of them
claims_you_doubt.why: Four deaths in a short window is too small a sample, and the source is an advocacy-linked group

questions_left_unanswered: How much do construction costs, labor, land prices and interest rates explain compared to the three locks?
Do 2-4 unit buildings actually need a second stair, given they're usually under 3 stories?
Why were 2-4 unit buildings still 1-in-13 homes if the locks are century-old? When did the decline really happen?
How do 2-4 unit buildings get financed now, and why does the 4-unit line hurt them if they're under it?
If Minneapolis and California reforms produced almost nothing, what would actually bring these buildings back?
best_moment: 08, because it puts the pro and anti evidence side by side (Minneapolis 317 units, SB 9 numbers, Auckland) and admits the record is mixed. It feels honest and makes the three-locks idea earn some credibility.
top3_fixes: Cut the history and stat-dumps in 02, 03 and 06 to one vivid example each (one Euclid quote, one Colorado number, one lending rule), and add a face or a real corner building the viewer can picture.

Fix the logic gap in 04 and 06: show how a typical 2-4 unit building runs into the stair and the lender line, since by the video's own facts it sits under the four-unit and three-story thresholds. Otherwise the locks don't apply to the building in the title.

Add the missing competing causes (construction costs, land prices, interest rates, developer economics) before claiming 'three locks' explain the decline, and make the ending match the weak reform results from 08 instead of ending on momentum.
